This general recommendation contributes to the growing body of international human rights standards on reparations and provides valuable guidance for states seeking to address enduring consequences of these historical injustices. The Permanent Forum has emphasized that reparatory justice is not solely about addressing historical wrongs. It is about confronting their continuing consequences and transforming the conditions that sustain inequality today. reparatory justice requires measures aimed at restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, guarantees of non-repetition, land justice, climate justice, digital justice, economic justice, and the restoration of dignity, among others. It requires acknowledging that many of the disparities experienced by people of African descent today are rooted in historical systems of exploitation, whose efforts remain visible across generations. Within this broader framework, the Permanent Forum devoted particular attention to cultural heritage and restitution in its annual session. The extraction of cultural property archives, sacred objects, and human remains formed an integral part of colonial domination. Restitution therefore constitutes an essential dimension of reparatory justice and of the realization of cultural rights. This is why the Permanent Forum calls for renewed efforts to facilitate the return of cultural property required during colonialism, to remove obstacles that continue to impede restitution processes, to integrate restitution into broader reparatory justice frameworks, and to ensure the meaningful participation of people of African descent in all decisions concerning the preservation, protection, and restitution of their cultural heritage. To reiterate, the Permanent Forum has recommended and called for a global conference on reparatory justice, an international study on the legal dimensions of reparatory justice, and the eventual establishment of an international mechanism to address reparatory justice. It has become the largest platform within the United Nations dedicated to discussing the human rights of people of African descent. Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, I have the honor to present to you the report of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights on education as a tool to prevent racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance pursuant to Human Rights Council resolution 57/24. The report examines four interconnected dimensions of formal education systems: governance and accountability, educational environments, curricula, pedagogies and educational materials, and finally the training and representation of teachers, authorities and educational personnel. Across each of these dimensions, the report synthesizes and analyzes existing state practices, measures, and challenges, drawing upon 135 submissions from states and to the stakeholders. The report starts from a simple but important premise. Education has enormous potential to prevent, challenge, and ultimately dismantle racism. as recognized by several international human rights treaties and instruments, including the Durban Declaration and Program of Action 25 years ago. At the same time, education systems can also reproduce and perpetuate racism. Indeed, in some contexts, education can be wielded as a tool for division, intolerance, resentment, racial abuse, and violence. and for spreading false notions of racial hierarchies and superiority. The report highlights that racism in education is not confined to isolated individual acts. Rather, it is embedded within educational systems, structures, and institutions. It is reflected in the exclusionary laws and policy, unequal opportunities, distorted curricula and educational content, unsafe school environments, and discriminatory institutional practices that produce unequal outcomes for children belonging to marginalized racial and ethnic groups. Ultimately, racism in education is a structural issue which requires a structural response. For this reason, the High Commission calls for human rights-based, transformative, child-centered and intersectional approach to dismantling racism that may be embedded across educational structures, institutions and systems. To this end, the report outlines some 20 concrete, targeted education-related practices and measures for States to undertake with a view to ensuring an inclusive, equitable and anti-racism education system. The High Commissioner also calls upon States to strengthen inclusive educational governance and accountability. States should adopt and effectively implement laws and policies prohibiting racial discrimination in education. They should also establish robust monitoring and accountability mechanisms, collect and analyze disaggregated data, and ensure the meaningful, safe, and inclusive participation of children, parents, teachers, and affected communities in educational decision-making. Additionally, creating safe, inclusive and child-friendly learning environments through anti-racism policies, reporting, investigation and redress mechanisms in cases of racial incidents, as well as protection and support systems for affected children, is critical. States must transform curricula, pedagogy, and educational materials to promote human rights, inclusion, and anti-racism. They should systematically audit and review curricula, pedagogies, and educational materials to eliminate negative stereotypes, biases, and historical distortion. States should also ensure that the diverse perspectives, histories, cultures, contributions, knowledge systems and agency of marginalized racial and ethnic groups are accurately reflected. The High Commissioner further underscores the importance of strengthening and expanding anti-racism education, multilingual and multicultural education and digital and media literacy. Finally, The High Commissioner recommends States to invest in the capacity of teachers and educational personnel by providing continuous training on human rights and inclusion, anti-racism, child protection and digital literacy. States should also ensure greater representation of marginalized racial and ethnic groups within the teaching and leadership roles. The way forward charted in this report can support Member States in partnership with national human rights institutions and civil society to safeguard the preventative potential of education and thus ensure more inclusive, equitable and anti-racist societies. Thank you.
